The 10 MW blade from the AVATAR project was used in the present investigation.
The simulations were conducted at a wind speed of 10.5 m/s and a rotational speed of 9.0218 rpm, with a pitch angle of 0.0°.
The CFD simulations were performed using the FLOWer code with the SST-kω turbulence model and a dual time-stepping approach.
Three different mesh sizes were used, with the medium mesh having 10.9 million cells.
The grid convergence index (GCI) was 0.003% for power and 0.0497% for thrust, indicating spatial convergence.
The FLOWer results showed very good agreement with the DTU EllipSys3D predictions, validating the CFD setup.
The 3D simulations showed a significant increase in the lift coefficient at the inboard section of the blade compared to the 2D simulations.
A delay in the separation point and a reduction in the wake size were observed at the inboard section of the 3D blade due to the centrifugal and Coriolis forces.
The rotational effects were most pronounced at the inboard section, with the augmentation becoming smaller towards the middle and tip regions of the blade.

The XFOIL calculations consistently showed higher lift coefficients compared to the CFD results, especially at the inboard sections, due to the limitations of the boundary layer code for thick airfoils.

The coarse mesh (8.1 million cells) underpredicted the sectional forces at the inboard section, while the medium (10.9 million cells) and fine (15.9 million cells) meshes produced very similar results.
The present results agree with previous studies that the rotation decreases the pressure level on the suction side of the blade, which increases the lift coefficient.
The findings from this study can help improve the accuracy of blade element momentum (BEM) models and inform the design of large wind turbine blades.
